mainEntity.name: Will a tongue piercing damage my dental implant crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is a genuine risk that a metal tongue bar or stud could cause wear, chipping, or abrasion to an implant crown, particularly over time with repeated contact during eating and speaking. Implant crowns are durable, but they are not indestructible. The extent of any risk will depend on the location of the implant, the type and size of the jewellery used, and individual habits such as playing with or biting the piercing. Your dental team can assess your specific situation during an examination and advise accordingly.

mainEntity.name: Can I get a lip piercing after dental implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Timing is important. During the initial healing phase following implant placement — which typically spans several months — introducing a lip piercing is generally not advisable, as it represents an additional source of potential infection and tissue irritation during a period when your body is working to integrate the implant. Once healing is confirmed and the implant is stable, the decision to proceed with a piercing can be discussed with your dental professional, who will advise based on your specific circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Can an oral piercing cause peri-implantitis?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no direct evidence that oral piercings cause peri-implantitis independently. However, any chronic source of infection or inflammation in the mouth may contribute to the overall bacterial environment. Peri-implantitis — an inflammatory condition affecting the tissue and bone surrounding an implant — has multiple contributing factors, including oral hygiene, smoking, and systemic health. An infected or inflamed piercing site is a factor worth considering and discussing with your dental team as part of a broader assessment of implant health.

mainEntity.name: What should I do if I notice swelling near my implant and I have an oral piercing?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you notice unexplained swelling, tenderness, or changes around your dental implant — particularly if you also have an oral piercing — it is advisable to seek a professional dental assessment without delay. It is not always possible to determine the cause of swelling without a clinical examination, and early assessment allows any concerns to be addressed promptly. Try not to self-diagnose based on internet research alone; a qualified dental professional is the most appropriate person to evaluate your symptoms.

mainEntity.name: Does the location of the piercing affect the level of risk to my implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, location is a relevant factor. A tongue piercing may pose a different set of concerns compared to a lip piercing, depending on the position of the dental implant. For example, a tongue bar is more likely to come into direct contact with the crowns of lower or upper posterior teeth and implants, whilst a lower lip piercing may more frequently affect the lower front gum margin. The specific implications for your oral health will depend on the location of your implant, the proposed piercing site, and your individual anatomy — all of which should be discussed with your dental professional.

mainEntity.name: Are there any types of piercing jewellery that are safer for implant patients?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some dental and piercing professionals suggest that softer, more flexible materials — such as PTFE (bioflex) — may reduce the risk of hard impact trauma to teeth and implants compared to rigid metal jewellery. Smaller jewellery sizes may also reduce the likelihood of contact with dental restorations. However, no jewellery material is entirely without risk within the oral environment, and any recommendation should take into account your individual circumstances. This is a conversation worth having with both your dental team and an experienced piercing professional before making any changes.
